metadata.title: Counterfactual Graph Representation Learning for Fairness-Aware Cognitive Diagnosis

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the PISA 2015 dataset and filters to students with at least 20 response records, then randomly splits the remaining data into training (70%), validation (10%), and test (20%). The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in model training or evaluation, nor does it name any weight variables from the PISA database. Because the proposed method is a deep learning architecture (GVAE + adversarial discriminator + Siamese network) trained with standard optimizers, the paper does not describe any weight-aware estimation procedure; thus, weighting is likely omitted. For analysts reproducing this work, the appropriate PISA student sampling weight(s) should be used if the goal is population-representative inference, and replicate weights should be used for uncertainty quantification; however, the paper’s reported metrics appear to be based on unweighted predictive performance.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are exercise response correctness/scores used in a cognitive diagnosis framework (cross-entropy loss on predicted response labels), rather than PV-based achievement scores. As a result, PISA plausible values are not the target of the prediction task, so PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not describe any explicit missing-data strategy for student contextual features or response records beyond the inclusion filter requiring at least 20 response records, which leaves the treatment of remaining missingness (if any) unclear; this is a reporting gap because missingness can affect graph construction and model training.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA 2015 and filters to include only students with at least 20 response records to ensure sufficient interactive data per student. The filtered dataset is then randomly split into training, validation, and test sets with a ratio of 70%:10%:20%. The paper does not report additional restrictions by grade, school type, or country subset, and it does not provide per-country sample counts.

main_findings.performance_metrics: FACD vs baselines (Table 4): IRT framework — ACC 0.7123, AUC 0.7853, RMSE 0.4179; MIRT — ACC 0.6734, AUC 0.7334, RMSE 0.4638; NeuralCDM — ACC 0.7212, AUC 0.7786, RMSE 0.4134; KaNCD — ACC 0.7221, AUC 0.7905, RMSE 0.4338. Fairness variants: Base+ generally decreases AUC (e.g., IRT AUC 0.7801→0.7729) while Reg improves but is below FACD (e.g., MIRT AUC 0.7179→0.7334; RMSE 0.4816→0.4638).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 the study leveraged student contextual features together with sensitive attributes (gender, geographic region, and family socioeconomic status) within a counterfactual graph representation learning pipeline to predict exercise response outcomes, finding that FACD achieved the best or near-best performance across ACC, AUC, and RMSE compared with IRT/MIRT/NeuralCDM/KaNCD and their fairness-aware variants. This indicates that fairness-aware counterfactual graph learning can improve diagnostic accuracy while reducing reliance on sensitive information, supporting the deployment of more equitable cognitive diagnosis models in intelligent education systems, though the paper does not provide causal identification beyond counterfactual representation constraints.

main_findings.target_variable: Fairness of prediction errors (GD-RMSE and EOD)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Fairness metrics (Table 5): FACD achieves lowest GD-RMSE and EOD across IRT, MIRT, NeuralCDM, and KaNCD. Examples: IRT — GD-RMSE 0.0214 (vs Base 0.0321, Reg 0.0288), EOD 0.0305 (vs Base 0.0452, Reg 0.0391); MIRT — GD-RMSE 0.0297 (vs Base 0.0416, Reg 0.0369), EOD 0.0374 (vs Base 0.0583, Reg 0.0488); NeuralCDM — GD-RMSE 0.0220, EOD 0.0298; KaNCD — GD-RMSE 0.0235, EOD 0.0312.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 the study leveraged student contextual features and sensitive attributes within a counterfactual fairness learning framework to predict exercise outcomes, finding that FACD produced the smallest group disparities in error (GD-RMSE) and the lowest equalized-odds differences (EOD) across multiple cognitive diagnosis backbones. This indicates that counterfactual graph representation learning can materially reduce demographic-group performance gaps in cognitive diagnosis systems, supporting policy and practice aimed at fairness-aware assessment design, while noting that the fairness metrics are predictive disparities rather than proof of causal fairness.

data.outcome_summary: The study proposes FACD, a fairness-aware cognitive diagnosis model using counterfactual graph representation learning, and evaluates it on PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) data. After filtering to students with at least 20 response records, the authors train on a 70/10/20 split and compare FACD against IRT, MIRT, NeuralCDM, and KaNCD as well as fairness variants (Base+ and Reg). Across frameworks, FACD attains the strongest overall predictive performance, with improvements in ACC/AUC and reductions in RMSE (e.g., under MIRT: AUC 0.7334 and RMSE 0.4638). For fairness, FACD consistently yields the lowest GD-RMSE and EOD values across backbones (e.g., IRT: GD-RMSE 0.0214, EOD 0.0305). Limitations include missing reporting on survey-weight usage and missing-data handling, and the fairness objective targets representation invariance rather than establishing causal effects.
